findings.title: Unguarded int() conversion on chunk length in chunked body reader may raise ValueError
findings.description: In `_read_chunked_body`, the chunk size string is parsed with `int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16)` without a try/except. If the client sends a non-hex value for the chunk length (e.g., an empty line, or text containing invalid hex characters), `int()` raises an unhandled `ValueError`. This exception is not caught anywhere in the call chain as an `httputil.HTTPInputError`, so it will propagate as an unhandled exception through the server request loop, causing the connection to be closed without a proper 400 response, and potentially logging an uncaught exception. A remote client can trigger this condition intentionally.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16)` call in a try/except ValueError block and raise `httputil.HTTPInputError` on failure, similar to how Content-Length is handled at line 612-619.

findings.title: assert used for protocol validation of chunk trailing CRLF in _read_chunked_body
findings.description: At line 687, `assert crlf == b"\r\n"` is used to validate that each chunk ends with the mandatory CRLF trailer. Using `assert` for protocol validation is incorrect because: (1) Python's `-O` optimization flag disables all asserts, silently bypassing the check; (2) when the assert fires (even in debug mode) it raises `AssertionError`, which is not caught by the `httputil.HTTPInputError` handler in `_read_message`. An `AssertionError` would propagate as an uncaught exception, logged at ERROR level and closing the connection abruptly rather than sending a 400 response.
findings.suggestion: Replace the assert with an explicit check that raises `httputil.HTTPInputError`: `if crlf != b"\r\n": raise httputil.HTTPInputError("improperly terminated chunk")`

findings.title: Negative Content-Length not rejected before size comparison
findings.description: At line 621, `content_length` is compared to `self._max_body_size` to enforce size limits. However, there is no check that `content_length` is non-negative. A client sending `Content-Length: -1` will pass the `int()` conversion at line 613 without raising an error, will pass the `> self._max_body_size` check (since -1 is not greater than any positive limit), and then in `_read_fixed_body` the while loop `while content_length > 0` will simply not execute, causing the connection to silently proceed as if there was no body — potentially bypassing application-level body processing logic.
findings.suggestion: Add a check `if content_length < 0: raise httputil.HTTPInputError('Negative Content-Length')` after parsing the integer value at line 613.

findings.title: HTTP response splitting: newline check only covers '\n' but not '\r' in header values
findings.description: At lines 447-449, the code checks for `b"\n"` in each header line but does not check for bare `b"\r"`. An attacker who can influence a header value containing `\r` followed by a subsequent header on the same logical line could potentially cause incorrect header parsing in downstream proxies or clients (HTTP response splitting / header injection via CR). While modern HTTP parsers typically handle this, the defense is incomplete — a `\r` without `\n` is not caught.
findings.suggestion: Also check for `b"\r"` in the header line validation: `if b"\n" in line or b"\r" in line: raise ValueError(...)`

findings.title: NameError: resp_start_line referenced before assignment when processing server-side body
findings.description: At line 253, `resp_start_line.code` is referenced unconditionally when `self.is_client` is False. However, `resp_start_line` is only assigned inside the `if self.is_client:` branch (line 200). When this code runs on the server side (`is_client=False`), `resp_start_line` is undefined in the local scope, causing an immediate `UnboundLocalError`. The ternary expression `resp_start_line.code if self.is_client else 0` is used, which in Python evaluates both branches syntactically but only executes the matching one at runtime — so when `is_client` is False, `resp_start_line.code` is NOT evaluated. This is actually safe due to Python's short-circuit evaluation of ternary expressions. Re-examining: Python evaluates `A if condition else B` — only A if condition is True, only B if False. So `resp_start_line.code` is only evaluated when `self.is_client` is True, which is the only case where it's defined. This is NOT a bug.
findings.suggestion: No action needed — Python's ternary conditional correctly avoids evaluating the unused branch.

findings.title: Potential decompression bomb (zip bomb) in gzip content decoding
findings.description: In `_GzipMessageDelegate.data_received`, gzip-compressed data is decompressed chunk-by-chunk. While each individual decompression call is limited to `self._chunk_size` bytes, the `while compressed_data` loop continues processing `unconsumed_tail` until all compressed data is processed. There is no limit on the total amount of decompressed data produced from a single compressed input stream. A malicious server (in client mode) or client (if server-side decompression is enabled) can send a highly compressed payload (zip bomb) that expands to gigabytes of memory, causing denial of service. The `_max_body_size` limit applies to the compressed Content-Length but not to the decompressed size.
findings.suggestion: Track total decompressed bytes and raise an error if the total exceeds `_max_body_size` or another configurable decompressed size limit.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` shared across all callers
findings.description: The parameter `exclude` in `serialize_response` defaults to `set()`, which is a mutable object. In Python, default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time and shared across all calls that use the default. If any caller mutates this set (e.g., by adding elements), subsequent calls that rely on the default will see the mutated set rather than an empty one. This can cause subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs where exclusions bleed across requests.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as the default and initialize the mutable container inside the function body: `exclude: Union[SetIntStr, DictIntStrAny] = None` and then `exclude = exclude or set()`.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` in `get_request_handler` shared across all callers
findings.description: The parameter `response_model_exclude` in `get_request_handler` defaults to `set()`. This mutable default is shared across all invocations that do not explicitly supply this argument. If the shared set is ever mutated, it could cause incorrect exclusion behavior across different route handlers.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as default and convert inside the function: `response_model_exclude = response_model_exclude or set()`.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` in `APIRoute.__init__` shared across all instances
findings.description: The `response_model_exclude` parameter of `APIRoute.__init__` defaults to `set()`. This mutable default is shared across all route instances that do not specify this argument. Mutation of this set in one route context could affect other route instances.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as default and initialize to `set()` inside the method body.

findings.title: Non-deterministic HTTP method selection for `unique_id` when multiple methods supplied
findings.description: On line 271, `list(methods)[0]` is called to pick the first HTTP method for generating the `unique_id`. However, `methods` at this point may still be the original input (a `Set[str]` or `List[str]`). If it is a `Set[str]`, converting to `list` does not guarantee any particular ordering. Additionally, the `self.methods` set is computed after this line (line 269), so the set's ordering may differ. This means the `unique_id` could vary non-deterministically across runs when multiple methods are provided as a set, leading to inconsistent OpenAPI operation IDs.
findings.suggestion: Sort the methods before picking the first one: `method=sorted(methods)[0]` or always normalize methods to a list first.

findings.title: Use of `assert` for runtime validation that can be disabled by Python optimization flag
findings.description: The `assert dependant.call is not None` statement on line 116 (and similarly at lines 136, 208, 275, 310, 313, 332, 522) performs a runtime safety check. However, when Python is run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, all `assert` statements are stripped and never executed. In a production environment using optimization, these safety guards are silently removed, potentially causing confusing `AttributeError` or `TypeError` exceptions downstream instead of clear error messages.
findings.suggestion: Replace `assert` with explicit `if` checks that raise appropriate exceptions (e.g., `ValueError` or `RuntimeError`) unconditionally.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` in `add_api_route` shared across all callers
findings.description: Multiple method signatures throughout the file (`add_api_route`, `api_route`, `get`, `put`, `post`, `delete`, `options`, `head`, `patch`, `trace`) use `set()` as a default value for `response_model_exclude`. All of these share the same mutable default object, creating a risk that mutations to one set will unexpectedly affect other route registrations.
findings.suggestion: Replace all `response_model_exclude: Union[SetIntStr, DictIntStrAny] = set()` defaults with `None` and initialize inside the function body.

findings.title: Overly broad empty-path guard in `include_router` only checks non-`APIRoute` routes
findings.description: When `prefix` is empty, the code iterates over all routes and raises an exception if a route has an empty `path`. However, this check only applies when `prefix` is falsy. Routes with a non-empty prefix bypass this check entirely, and the logic uses `getattr(r, 'path')` which will raise `AttributeError` if a route does not have a `path` attribute (since no default is provided for `getattr` with a missing attribute). Furthermore, the condition `if path is not None and not path` correctly catches the empty-string case, but `getattr(r, 'path')` without a default will raise `AttributeError` for route types that don't have a `path` attribute (e.g., `Mount`).
findings.suggestion: Use `getattr(r, 'path', None)` with a default of `None` to safely handle routes without a `path` attribute.

findings.title: JSON body parsed without size limit allowing potential DoS
findings.description: When a non-form body is expected, the code reads the entire request body with `await request.body()` and then calls `await request.json()` if the body is non-empty. There is no size limit enforced at this level. An attacker can send an extremely large JSON body, causing excessive memory consumption and CPU usage (parsing a huge JSON document). While Starlette/uvicorn may have their own limits that can be configured, the routing layer itself imposes no guard, so a misconfigured or default deployment is vulnerable.
findings.suggestion: Enforce a maximum body size at the server or middleware level, and document that body size limits must be configured. Consider adding a body size check before parsing JSON.

findings.title: Non-deterministic HTTP method selection for unique_id generation
findings.description: At line 316, `list(methods)[0]` is used to pick the first HTTP method for generating a unique operation ID. However, `methods` at this point may be a `Set[str]` or `List[str]` passed by the caller. When it is a set, the first element selected by `list(set)[0]` is non-deterministic across Python versions and runs (sets are unordered). This means the `unique_id` (and consequently the OpenAPI operation ID and the `response_name` derived from it) can vary between restarts or Python versions, leading to inconsistent OpenAPI schemas and potentially duplicate IDs if two routes share methods in different set orderings.
findings.suggestion: Sort the methods before picking the first one, e.g., `list(sorted(self.methods))[0]`, to ensure deterministic unique ID generation. Note that `self.methods` (line 314) is already converted to a set, so use `self.methods` consistently or sort before converting.

findings.title: Missing `from e` in JSONDecodeError re-raise loses exception chaining
findings.description: At line 186, `raise RequestValidationError([ErrorWrapper(e, ("body", e.pos))], body=e.doc)` is raised inside an `except json.JSONDecodeError as e` block without `raise ... from e`. This suppresses the original exception context, making debugging harder because the traceback chain is broken. The Ruff B904 rule flags this, and it constitutes a functional defect in error reporting.
findings.suggestion: Change the raise statement to use explicit chaining: `raise RequestValidationError([ErrorWrapper(e, ("body", e.pos))], body=e.doc) from e`.

findings.title: Use of `assert` for runtime enforcement that can be disabled with -O flag
findings.description: Multiple `assert` statements (lines 145, 167, 246, 320, 355, 358, 379) are used to enforce runtime invariants and preconditions. When Python is run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, all `assert` statements are stripped, bypassing these checks entirely. For example, `assert dependant.call is not None` at line 145 would silently allow a None call through, leading to an `AttributeError` or `TypeError` at a later point. In production environments where optimization flags may be used, this causes unhandled exceptions rather than meaningful error messages.
findings.suggestion: Replace `assert` with explicit `if` checks and raise appropriate exceptions (e.g., `ValueError` or `RuntimeError`) for invariants that must hold at runtime.

findings.title: Use of `assert` for input validation bypassed by Python optimization mode
findings.description: The prefix validation in `APIRouter.__init__` uses `assert` statements (lines 436-439) to enforce that the path prefix starts with '/' and does not end with '/'. When Python is run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, all `assert` statements are stripped from the bytecode, meaning these checks are completely skipped. An invalid prefix (e.g., one not starting with '/') would then be silently accepted, leading to malformed route paths that could break routing or OpenAPI schema generation.
findings.suggestion: Replace `assert` with explicit `if` checks that raise `ValueError` (or another appropriate exception) to ensure validation always occurs regardless of Python's optimization mode.

findings.title: Use of `assert` for prefix validation in `include_router` bypassed by Python optimization mode
findings.description: The `include_router` method also uses `assert` statements (lines 614-617) to validate that the `prefix` argument starts with '/' and does not end with '/'. These checks are eliminated when Python is run with `-O`, allowing malformed prefixes to silently pass through and cause incorrect route registration or URL construction.

findings.title: Incorrect operator precedence in autoescape condition causes wrong branch selection
findings.description:
The condition at line 201-205 is:
```python
if (
    hasattr(old, "__html__")
    or hasattr(new, "__html__")
    and not hasattr(s, "__html__")
):
```
Due to Python's operator precedence, `and` binds tighter than `or`, so this is evaluated as:
```python
if hasattr(old, "__html__") or (hasattr(new, "__html__") and not hasattr(s, "__html__")):
```
This means when `old` has `__html__` but `s` also has `__html__`, the code still takes the `if` branch and calls `escape(s)` even though `s` is already HTML-safe (has `__html__`). The intended logic was likely:
```python
if (hasattr(old, "__html__") or hasattr(new, "__html__")) and not hasattr(s, "__html__"):
```
Which would only escape `s` if a replacement operand is Markup-aware AND `s` itself is not. The incorrect logic can lead to `s` being escaped (and thus double-escaped) when it shouldn't be, or the wrong branch being taken.
findings.suggestion:
Use explicit parentheses to clarify intent:
```python
if (
    (hasattr(old, "__html__") or hasattr(new, "__html__"))
    and not hasattr(s, "__html__")
):
```

findings.title: LIKE pattern injection via unescaped wildcard characters in filter functions
findings.description: The filter functions mysql_contains, mysql_starts_with, mysql_ends_with, and their case-insensitive variants interpolate the `value` parameter directly into LIKE patterns using f-strings (e.g., `f"%{value}%"`). If `value` contains SQL LIKE wildcard metacharacters `%` or `_`, they will be interpreted as wildcards by the MySQL engine rather than as literal characters. This allows an attacker to craft filter values that match unintended rows, effectively bypassing exact-match semantics. For example, a `contains` filter with value `%` would match every row, and a value like `a_c` would match 'abc', 'aXc', etc. The characters `%`, `_`, and `\` must be escaped before embedding in LIKE patterns.
findings.suggestion: Escape LIKE metacharacters in `value` before interpolation. Replace `%` with `\%`, `_` with `\_`, and `\` with `\\`. For example: `escaped = value.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')` and then use `f"%{escaped}%"`. Alternatively, use parameterized LIKE patterns with the database driver's escaping support.

findings.title: HTTPNotFound raised as class instead of instance
findings.description: On line 670, `raise HTTPNotFound` raises the class itself rather than an instance of it (`raise HTTPNotFound()`). In Python, raising a class that is not an exception instance works for built-in exceptions but for custom exception classes derived from HTTPException (which inherit from Exception), this will typically cause a TypeError at runtime because the class is not instantiated. This means that when a static file path exists but is neither a file nor a directory, the server will crash with a TypeError instead of returning a proper 404 response.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPNotFound` to `raise HTTPNotFound()` to properly instantiate the exception before raising it.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unsanitized file names in directory listing
findings.description: The `_directory_as_html` method on line 672 generates an HTML directory listing that directly embeds file names and paths into HTML without any HTML entity escaping. On line 697, `file_name` is inserted directly into an HTML anchor tag's text content, and on line 696, `file_url` (derived from `_prefix + "/" + rel_path`) is inserted into the `href` attribute. If a file or directory on the filesystem has a name containing HTML special characters (e.g., `<script>alert(1)</script>.txt`), this would result in stored XSS when the directory listing is rendered in a browser. findings.title: Path traversal bypass possible in url_for version appending when follow_symlinks is False

The `filename` comes from `str(filename).lstrip("/")` on line 566 which only strips leading slashes but does not prevent `..` sequences. A path like `../../etc/passwd` after lstrip would still contain `..` and could potentially escape the directory, though `resolve()` mitigates direct traversal. The concern is that the error is silently swallowed rather than raising an error.

An attacker with the ability to register routes (e.g., via a configuration file or admin interface) could provide a catastrophically backtracking regex pattern. findings.title: Path traversal via os.path.normpath on root-anchored paths
findings.description: The `get_path` method splits the scope path on '/' and joins it with `os.path.join(*parts)`. When the scope path is '/', `split('/')` returns `['', '']`, and `os.path.join('', '')` returns `''`, which `os.path.normpath` turns into `'.'`. More critically, if the path begins with '/', the first element of the split is an empty string and `os.path.join` ignores all preceding components when it encounters an absolute path component. For example, a path like `//etc/passwd` could produce unexpected results. While `lookup_path` uses `commonprefix` as a secondary guard, the path normalization in `get_path` is the first line of defense and has subtle edge cases. The use of `os.path.normpath(os.path.join(*scope['path'].split('/')))` does not reliably strip leading slashes or handle edge cases like paths containing null bytes on some systems.
findings.suggestion: Use `pathlib.PurePosixPath` to parse the URL path and then convert to a relative path safely, e.g., `path = str(pathlib.PurePosixPath(scope['path']).relative_to('/'))` combined with stripping leading separators. Alternatively, ensure the result of `get_path` is always a relative path by checking it doesn't start with the OS separator.

findings.title: Path traversal bypass via commonprefix directory check
findings.description: `os.path.commonprefix` operates on raw strings, not path components. This means a directory `/srv/static` and a path `/srv/static_evil/secret.txt` would share the common prefix `/srv/static`, causing the check `os.path.commonprefix([full_path, directory]) != directory` to incorrectly pass (evaluate as equal to `directory`), thereby allowing access to files outside the intended static directory. An attacker who can craft a request path that resolves to a sibling directory starting with the same string as the static directory could bypass this path containment check.
findings.suggestion: Replace the `commonprefix` check with a proper path prefix check that operates on path components. Use `pathlib.Path`: `pathlib.Path(full_path).is_relative_to(pathlib.Path(directory))` (Python 3.9+), or manually check that the full path starts with `directory + os.sep` or equals `directory`.

findings.title: PermissionError mapped to HTTP 401 instead of HTTP 403
findings.description: When a `PermissionError` is raised during `lookup_path` (e.g., because the process lacks read permission on a file or directory), the code raises `HTTPException(status_code=401)`, which means 'Unauthorized' (authentication required). The correct HTTP status code for a permission/access denial is 403 'Forbidden'. Using 401 may confuse clients into attempting authentication when the resource is simply forbidden regardless of credentials.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPException(status_code=401)` to `raise HTTPException(status_code=403)` to correctly signal that access is forbidden rather than that authentication is needed.

findings.title: NoneAlgorithm.verify() always returns False instead of True
findings.description: The NoneAlgorithm.verify() method unconditionally returns False. For the 'none' algorithm, verification should succeed (return True) when the signature is an empty byte string, since no cryptographic verification is needed. Returning False means any JWT using alg='none' will always fail signature verification, which may cause callers to fall through to insecure bypass logic or create inconsistent behavior depending on how the calling code handles a False return versus an exception. However, note that the 'none' algorithm itself is a security risk and should typically be explicitly disallowed; but if it is registered and used, its verify() logic is broken.
findings.suggestion: Change verify() to return True when sig == b'' (i.e., when the signature matches the expected empty signature for the none algorithm). Better still, ensure the 'none' algorithm is removed from default algorithms or guarded by strict configuration.

findings.title: RSAPSSAlgorithm uses hash_alg.digest_size as salt_length, which is incorrect for PSS
findings.description: In RSAPSSAlgorithm.sign() and verify(), the PSS salt_length is set to `self.hash_alg.digest_size`. However, `self.hash_alg` is a class (e.g., `hashes.SHA256`), not an instance, so `self.hash_alg.digest_size` accesses the class attribute. More critically, the standard practice for RSASSA-PSS (as specified in RFC 7518 for PS256/PS384/PS512) requires the salt length to equal the hash output length. While `digest_size` as a class attribute may work for some versions of the cryptography library, the canonical way is to use `padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH` or to instantiate the hash and get its digest size. Additionally, a mismatch between signing salt_length and verification salt_length (both set to `hash_alg.digest_size`) means that if an external signer used a different salt length, verification will fail even for legitimately signed tokens.
findings.suggestion: Use `padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH` for the salt_length in verify() (to accept any valid salt), and `self.hash_alg().digest_size` (instantiated) for signing. Alternatively, use `self.hash_alg.digest_size` only if confirmed to be a stable class-level attribute in the cryptography library version used.

findings.title: Malformed error message string in ECAlgorithm.from_jwk()
findings.description: At line 506, the InvalidKeyError is raised with the format string `"D should be {} bytes for curve {}"` along with positional arguments `len(x)` and `curve`, but InvalidKeyError (likely an Exception subclass) does not support `.format()`-style argument interpolation via positional args to the constructor. The arguments `len(x)` and `curve` are passed as additional constructor arguments and will be silently ignored, resulting in an error message that literally reads `"D should be {} bytes for curve {}"` with unfilled placeholders.
findings.suggestion: Use an f-string or explicit .format() call: `raise InvalidKeyError(f"D should be {len(x)} bytes for curve {curve}")`

findings.title: RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key() silently swallows UnsupportedAlgorithm and other exceptions during key loading
findings.description: In RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key(), only ValueError is caught when attempting to load the key as a private PEM key. If load_pem_private_key() raises a different exception (e.g., cryptography.exceptions.UnsupportedAlgorithm, TypeError, or other errors), it will propagate uncaught. Similarly, the fallback to load_pem_public_key() is only triggered on ValueError, meaning non-RSA PEM keys that trigger other exceptions during private key loading will produce confusing errors rather than a clear InvalidKeyError.
findings.suggestion: Broaden the exception handling to include additional exception types from the cryptography library (e.g., UnsupportedAlgorithm) and raise InvalidKeyError with a clear message in all failure cases.

findings.title: RSAAlgorithm.to_jwk() uses fragile duck-typing checks that may produce incorrect results
findings.description: The check `getattr(key_obj, 'private_numbers', None)` on line 271 checks for the existence of the attribute, which evaluates to the bound method (truthy). However, RSAPublicKey objects also have a `verify` method (line 288 uses `getattr(key_obj, 'verify', None)`). The logic will work for standard RSA key objects, but if any key-like object has a `private_numbers` attribute that is not callable or is falsy, it will incorrectly fall through to the public key branch or raise InvalidKeyError. Additionally, the `verify` attribute check on line 288 may match non-RSA objects that also have a `verify` method.
findings.suggestion: Use isinstance() checks with RSAPrivateKey and RSAPublicKey instead of duck-typing with getattr().

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized name_filter in ILIKE query
findings.description: The `name_filter` parameter is taken directly from user input via `self.get_argument("name_filter", None)` and interpolated into an `ilike` ORM filter using an f-string: `orm.User.name.ilike(f'%{name_filter}%')`. While SQLAlchemy's `ilike` with string literals is parameterized at the SQL level, the `%` wildcards are concatenated into the pattern string itself. However, the real risk is that the value is not sanitized at all — a user can inject SQL wildcard characters (`%`, `_`) to alter the matching behavior, effectively turning an exact-prefix search into an arbitrary pattern scan across all usernames. This is a SQL wildcard injection issue that can expose all usernames regardless of intended filtering scope.
findings.suggestion: Escape SQLAlchemy-level wildcard characters in `name_filter` before use (e.g., replace `%` with `\%` and `_` with `\_` and pass `escape='\\'` to `ilike`), or use `contains()` with proper escaping.

findings.title: NoneType AttributeError when current_user is a Service in delete handler
findings.description: At line 286, the delete handler compares `user.name == self.current_user.name`. The `current_user` could be an `orm.Service` object (not a `User`), which may not have a `.name` attribute in the same way, or could be `None` if the auth check somehow passes. While `@needs_scope('delete:users')` guard is present, if `self.current_user` is a Service object, accessing `.name` could still work, but the semantic comparison — checking if the user being deleted is the requester — is flawed because a Service could never be the same as a User object, making the guard trivially bypassable (a service could delete any user). The deeper issue is that `self.current_user` may be an `orm.Service`, which has a different type than `User`, and comparing by name alone is not a meaningful identity check in this context.
findings.suggestion: Check both that the current_user is a User (not a Service) and that names match: `isinstance(self.current_user, User) and user.name == self.current_user.name`. Also handle the case where `self.current_user` might be None.

findings.title: Use of naive datetime for token expiry comparison (timezone-unaware)
findings.description: At line 357, `now = datetime.utcnow()` creates a timezone-naive datetime. At line 364, this is compared against `token.expires_at`. If `token.expires_at` is stored as a timezone-aware datetime (e.g., with UTC timezone info), this comparison will raise a `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Conversely, if both are naive, the comparison is correct but fragile. This is the same issue as comparing apples to oranges in terms of datetime awareness.
findings.suggestion: Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` for a timezone-aware comparison, or ensure that `token.expires_at` is always stored as a naive UTC datetime. Apply the same fix as `_parse_timestamp` does at line 808.

findings.title: Mass assignment via unrestricted setattr in patch handler
findings.description: In `UserAPIHandler.patch` (lines 325-331), the code iterates over all keys in the request body `data` and calls `setattr(user, key, value)` for any key that is not `auth_state`. The reliance on `_check_user_model` to block all dangerous keys needs verification, but the pattern of `setattr` over arbitrary dict keys is inherently risky.
findings.suggestion: Use an explicit whitelist of allowed settable fields (e.g., `{'name', 'admin', 'auth_state'}`) rather than iterating over all keys in the data dict with `setattr`.

findings.title: Incorrect truncation warning: compares post-limit query count to total
findings.description: At line 169, `query_count = query.count()` counts the results of the already-offset and limited query (because `query` has `.offset(offset).limit(limit)` applied at line 156). Comparing this limited count against `total_count` will always show the page size vs total, not whether the response was truncated. The condition `total_count > query_count` will almost always be true when `total_count > limit`, even for the first page with exactly `limit` results. This leads to spurious truncation warnings for normal paginated data.
findings.suggestion: The truncation check should compare `total_count > limit` (or `total_count > len(user_list)`) rather than `total_count > query_count`. Alternatively, use `full_query.count()` which already exists for this purpose.

findings.title: LocalCache.__setitem__ crashes with TypeError when limit is None
findings.description: In LocalCache.__setitem__, the condition `while len(self) >= self.limit` is evaluated unconditionally. When `limit=None` (the default value), Python raises `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'`. The docstring and constructor signature imply that `limit=None` is a valid state (meaning no limit), but the __setitem__ method does not guard against this. Any attempt to insert an item into a LocalCache with no limit will raise a TypeError instead of behaving as an unlimited cache.
findings.suggestion: Add a guard check before the while loop: `if self.limit is not None:` wrapping the eviction logic, so that a None limit means unlimited capacity.

findings.title: MultiValueDict.__deepcopy__ calls __init__ without arguments, triggering deprecation warning recursively and bypassing initialization
findings.description: In `__deepcopy__`, `self.__class__()` is called with no arguments. Since `MultiValueDict.__init__` requires `key_to_list_mapping` (defaulting to `()`) and emits a deprecation warning on every instantiation, this causes an unexpected additional deprecation warning to be emitted during deep-copy operations. While not a crash, it is a functional defect where the copy internally triggers unwanted side effects (extra warnings) that can confuse users. Additionally, the `copy()` method calls `self.__deepcopy__()` directly without passing a `memo` dict, which is a minor deviation from the deepcopy protocol but works here since memo defaults to `{}`.
findings.suggestion: Consider bypassing `__init__` during deepcopy by using `object.__new__(self.__class__)` and then calling `dict.__init__` directly, or suppress the deprecation warning during internal copy operations.

findings.title: CaselessDict.get normalizes the default value unnecessarily
findings.description: In `CaselessDict.get`, the default value is passed through `self.normvalue(def_val)` before being returned as a default. This is semantically incorrect: if the caller passes a specific default value (e.g., `False`, `0`, or a custom object), it should be returned as-is, not transformed by normvalue. If a subclass overrides `normvalue` to perform type coercion or transformation, the default value would be silently altered when the key is absent, leading to unexpected behavior.
findings.suggestion: Change the `get` method to not normalize the default value: `return dict.get(self, self.normkey(key), def_val)`. The normalization of defaults is a logical error; only stored values should be normalized via `normvalue`.

findings.title: CaselessDict.__init__ skips update when seq is falsy but non-None
findings.description: The condition `if seq:` in `CaselessDict.__init__` will skip calling `self.update(seq)` when `seq` is any falsy value, including an empty dict `{}`, an empty list `[]`, or `0`. While an empty collection would result in no items being added regardless, passing a custom falsy mapping object (e.g., a Mapping subclass that evaluates to False but contains items) would silently skip initialization. The correct check should be `if seq is not None:` to faithfully handle all edge cases.
findings.suggestion: Replace `if seq:` with `if seq is not None:` to ensure all non-None sequences are processed, including empty ones (which are harmless to process).

findings.title: StringAgg delimiter injected unsanitized into SQL template via string interpolation
findings.description: The `StringAgg` class embeds the `delimiter` parameter directly into the SQL template string using Python's `%`-style string formatting: `"%(function)s(%(distinct)s%(expressions)s, '%(delimiter)s'%(ordering)s)"`. The delimiter value is passed by the caller at construction time and is interpolated verbatim into the SQL fragment. A delimiter containing a single-quote character (e.g., `delimiter="'; DROP TABLE users; --"`) can break out of the surrounding SQL string literal and inject arbitrary SQL, leading to SQL injection. Because the template is rendered before parameterization, the delimiter is never treated as a bound parameter by the database driver.
findings.suggestion: Do not embed the delimiter directly in the SQL template string. Instead, pass the delimiter as a parameterized query argument (e.g., use `%s` placeholder and supply the value through the database driver's parameter binding mechanism), or at minimum validate/escape the delimiter to ensure it cannot contain SQL-special characters such as single quotes.

findings.title: ArrayAgg.convert_value treats empty list and None identically due to falsy check
findings.description: The `convert_value` method in `ArrayAgg` uses `if not value:` to guard against null/empty results. This truthiness check conflates two distinct cases: (1) the database returning NULL (Python `None`) and (2) the database returning an empty array `[]`. In the latter case, PostgreSQL's `ARRAY_AGG` can legitimately return an empty list, but `not []` is `True` in Python, so an empty array result would be replaced with a new `[]` instead of being passed through — while functionally equivalent here, the check masks the actual NULL vs. empty distinction. More critically, if future callers depend on detecting `None` vs `[]` for NULL handling (e.g., when used with `FILTER` clauses that truly produce NULL), the incorrect masking would silently return `[]` instead of signaling no data.
findings.suggestion: Use an explicit `if value is None:` check instead of `if not value:` to distinguish between a NULL result from the database and a legitimately empty array result. This makes the intent explicit and avoids masking edge cases.

findings.title: JSONBAgg.convert_value treats None and empty list identically due to falsy check
findings.description: Same pattern as `ArrayAgg.convert_value`: `if not value:` will be `True` for both `None` (database NULL) and `[]` (empty JSON array). Using `if value is None:` would correctly distinguish these cases. findings.title: Unbounded method string passed to _hash_internal without validation
findings.description: In check_password_hash, the method field is extracted from pwhash via split('$', 2) and passed directly to _hash_internal without any pre-validation. While _hash_internal does raise ValueError for unknown methods, a maliciously crafted stored hash could contain a method like 'scrypt:9999999999:9999999999:9999999999' causing _hash_internal to compute an extraordinarily large maxmem value (132 * n * r * p), potentially leading to a denial-of-service through memory exhaustion. The scrypt parameters n, r, p are accepted from the stored hash with no upper bound checks.
findings.suggestion: Validate scrypt parameters (n, r, p) against reasonable maximum values before computing maxmem or calling hashlib.scrypt. For example, cap n at 2**20, r at 64, and p at 16. Consider also validating pbkdf2 iterations against a reasonable maximum.

findings.title: safe_join may not detect traversal via posixpath.normpath resolving to '..'
findings.description: After calling posixpath.normpath(filename), the code checks if the result equals '..' or starts with '../'. However, posixpath.normpath can produce paths that begin with multiple '..' components such as '../../etc/passwd' which would be caught by the startswith('../') check. However, if filename is an empty string (filename == ''), normpath is skipped entirely and '' is appended to parts. While an empty part in posixpath.join is benign, the bypass of normpath means other edge cases might exist. More critically, on Windows systems, _os_alt_seps includes backslash, but the check only covers known alt separators. A path like '..' passed through normpath remains '..' and is caught. However, paths like 'foo/../../bar' normalize to '../bar' which starts with '../' and is caught. The logic appears mostly correct, but the empty string bypass of normpath deserves scrutiny: posixpath.join with an empty string component is a no-op, so this seems safe.
findings.suggestion: Consider applying normpath even to empty strings (or simply skip empty filenames), and add a post-join check that the final path starts with the base directory. Using os.path.realpath on the final joined path and verifying it starts with the realpath of directory would provide stronger guarantees.

findings.title: RecipientFieldForTypingEditDirectMessage constructed with filtered user_ids instead of full participant list
findings.description: In `do_send_direct_message_edit_typing_notification`, `user_ids_to_notify` is computed by filtering out inactive users and those who have disabled typing notifications (lines 189-193). This filtered list is then used as the `user_ids` argument to `RecipientFieldForTypingEditDirectMessage` (line 195). However, the recipient field is meant to identify the direct message conversation (i.e., all participants), not just the notification targets. Using the filtered list means the recipient field will omit inactive or notification-disabled participants, causing the event to describe a different (potentially nonexistent) conversation than the actual one. This could confuse clients trying to correlate the event with the correct message thread. The original `user_ids` parameter (all participants) should be used to construct the recipient, while `user_ids_to_notify` is used only for delivery.
findings.suggestion: Construct `RecipientFieldForTypingEditDirectMessage` using the original `user_ids` list (all participants), not the filtered `user_ids_to_notify`. For example: `recipient = RecipientFieldForTypingEditDirectMessage(type='direct', user_ids=user_ids)`. The filtered `user_ids_to_notify` should only be passed to `send_event_rollback_unsafe`.

findings.title: Missing error handling for invalid user IDs in do_send_direct_message_edit_typing_notification
findings.description: In `do_send_direct_message_edit_typing_notification` (lines 184-186), `get_user_by_id_in_realm_including_cross_realm` is called without a try/except block. If any `user_id` in `user_ids` does not exist, a `UserProfile.DoesNotExist` exception will propagate unhandled to the caller. By contrast, `check_send_typing_notification` (lines 75-83) properly catches this exception and raises a `JsonableError` with a user-friendly message. The inconsistency means this function can throw an unexpected exception that may not be properly handled by the caller, potentially causing a 500 error instead of a 400 error response.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `get_user_by_id_in_realm_including_cross_realm` call in a try/except block similar to `check_send_typing_notification`, catching `UserProfile.DoesNotExist` and raising `JsonableError(_('Invalid user ID {user_id}').format(user_id=user_id)) from None`.

findings.title: Exception chaining suppression: raise without 'from' in except clause
findings.description: On line 82, within an `except UserProfile.DoesNotExist` clause, a new `JsonableError` is raised without using `raise ... from err` or `raise ... from None`. This means Python will implicitly chain the exceptions, attaching the original `DoesNotExist` as `__context__`, which can leak internal implementation details (model names, query details) in tracebacks visible to developers/logs. Using `raise ... from None` explicitly suppresses the chaining when that is the intent, making the intent clear and preventing unintentional context leakage.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise JsonableError(...)` to `raise JsonableError(_('Invalid user ID {user_id}').format(user_id=user_id)) from None` to explicitly suppress exception chaining.
